messages.text:
I need your help coming up with a new GDD for all graphics visual aspects of the game following real Human art principles to make this game less of a flat and bland copy-paste indie game look to something truly stylized and artistically composed. Actual instructions for Claude Code to follow in VS Code.

[8 private attachments omitted]

Apocky, this is a fantastic direction — studying *how humans actually learned to draw* and translating those principles into SDF shader instructions. Let me first absorb your existing visual docs to understand the current baseline, then I'll do a deep research dive into Renaissance art pedagogy, form construction, and how those principles map to procedural rendering.

Now let me look at the reference image you uploaded:

Alright Apocky, I've absorbed all seven of your existing visual docs — the Visual Bible, Aesthetic Style Guide, Visual Design Language, Illuminated Codex (all 13 phases complete), Design Reference, and Implementation Plan. Your rendering pipeline is sophisticated and your aesthetic systems are well-designed. But you're identifying the real gap: all of those docs tell the engine *how to render* but none of them teach Claude Code *how to see like an artist*.

The missing piece is the foundational layer — the same principles a Renaissance apprentice spent years internalizing: constructive anatomy, gesture drawing, weight distribution, form turning, proportional systems, compositional geometry, atmospheric perspective as understood by painters (not just shader parameters), and how to compose convincing forms from simple primitives *because you understand the underlying structure, not just the math*.

Let me do a deep research dive into this — studying how Renaissance masters and classical art pedagogy built convincing forms from geometric primitives, and how those principles translate directly into SDF composition rules.

Your Renaissance art principles for SDF composition report is ready. It covers the full construction pipeline—from gesture curves and proportional systems to shape language, lighting, and balance—translating classical figure drawing pedagogy into concrete SDF primitive composition rules. The report includes head-unit proportion tables, stylization mappings, archetype recipes for common game characters (brute, mage, rogue, child, monster), and practical parameters for smooth blending, silhouette testing, and value structure.

[1 private attachment omitted]
Now for the splash screen and all menus and UI's and fonts.

Now let me research the specific typographic, manuscript, and UI art direction principles to make this doc deeply grounded:

Now I have all the research and context. Let me build the GDD. This is a massive document so I'll use the docx skill for proper output:

Now I'll create the comprehensive GDD. Given the scope and that this is meant as instructions for Claude Code (not a Word deliverable), I'll create it as a markdown [redacted:file-uri]

Here's your **UI Renaissance Art Bible** — 639 lines, ~8,500 words of actual art-principled instructions for Claude Code.

The document bridges the gap between your existing `UI_MENU_DESIGN_BIBLE.md` (which tells the engine *what* to render) and the artistic knowledge needed to make it look *designed rather than assembled*. It covers:

**Part I** diagnoses exactly why game menus look like programmer art through Renaissance lens — no gesture, no hierarchy of form, no negative space design, no material truth, no typographic craft.

**Part II** gives concrete composition rules for every screen type: the asymmetric golden-section grid, the 2–3 mass "big shape" test, leading lines for eye flow, and the Notan value structure (60-25-15 dark-mid-light).

**Part III** is a complete typography system — five laws of game type, specific font stack requirements with candidate fonts (Cinzel, Crimson Pro, Inter, JetBrains Mono), the five-level typographic hierarchy with modular golden-ratio sizing, and the codex ink-color derivation system that ensures text feels *written on parchment* not *displayed on screen*.

**Part IV** gives screen-by-screen art direction: boot splash as "the book opens," title screen as "the frontispiece" with Renaissance composition analysis, HUD as "running marginalia," inventory as "bestiary plate," loading as "interleaf."

**Parts V–VII** cover material truth for panels, animation as calligraphy (every motion is a mark being made), and specific MSDF atlas generation parameters with shader enhancement specs.

**Part VIII** is a validation checklist ending with the ultimate test: show the title screen to someone and if they say "a book" or "something illustrated" rather than "a game menu," you've passed.

This pairs with the entity-level `RENAISSANCE_ART_PRINCIPLES_FOR_SDF.md` from the research artifact — together they give Claude Code the complete artistic education from figure drawing through page composition.

[redacted:local-path] Infinite Labyrinth

I need you to evaluate the codebase and tell me where I am going wrong in both the realtime action roguelike/looter-shooter gameplay as well as the Menu/UI/Graphics/Art because the game is technically sound but looks and feels bad and it is difficult to explain to the AI agent in VS Code, there is a fundamental disconnect in communication.
Let me dig into your actual codebase to see what's really happening versus what the specs describe. I'll use the filesystem tools to audit the code directly.
